# TADA at a glance {#tada}

**T**ransferable, **A**vailable, **D**ocumented, **A**nnotated. Four steps that
take analytical code from "on my laptop" to "runnable by a stranger in five
years".

## Why a fifth set of guidelines? {#tada-why}

There is no shortage of advice on writing good code. The problem is that almost
none of it is about *archiving an analysis*.

The TADA authors identify three specific gaps in the existing resources:

1. They do not sufficiently address **how to archive analytical code**.
2. Few of them adhere to the **FAIR principles**.
3. Those that do — notably **FAIR4RS**, the FAIR principles for Research
   Software — are broad in scope and aimed at **software developers**, which
   may be part of why they have not been widely adopted by researchers.

The distinction that makes this matter is between *analytical code* and
*software*:

> **Software** is written to be general, modular, tested, and to work across
> systems with many different compatible datasets. Designing for that kind of
> reuse is genuinely complicated.
>
> **Analytical code** is tailored to one dataset and one study. Its purpose is
> to be a transparent, reproducible record of that analysis — not to become a
> tool for other people.

Holding analytical code to software standards sets the bar too high, and the
result is that people clear neither bar. TADA sets a **minimum standard** that
is achievable for researchers at any coding level, and that still delivers the
transparency and computational reproducibility the sharing was for.

## The scale of the problem {#tada-problem}

The numbers behind that argument, all from the TADA paper's review of the
literature:

| What | Figure |
|---|---|
| Journals in ecology & evolutionary biology with code-sharing policies | 15% in 2015 → **88% in 2024** |
| Articles in the field with open code | **5–33%**, depending on the study |
| Archived R files in Harvard Dataverse failing to run without error | **74%** (falling to 56% after automated cleaning) |
| Scripts in species distribution/abundance papers that did not run, or ran with errors | **93%** |
| Meta-analyses computationally reproducible given working data and code | **27%** (all results matched exactly) to **73%** (half of results within 10%) |

Policies have moved. Practice has not followed. And even where code is present
and functional, computational reproducibility is not guaranteed.

## The four principles {#tada-four}

Each has its own chapter. This is the one-paragraph version of each.

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[T]{.tada-letter} [Transferable](#transferable){.tada-word}
[Anyone can **open the file, view it and run it** without conversion or
alteration — on a different computer and a different operating system. Standard
file extensions; no local file paths.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Available](#available){.tada-word}
[The code is **publicly archived** so that any external user has long-term
access to it, with a **globally unique persistent identifier** (e.g. a DOI)
that is cited in the manuscript.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[D]{.tada-letter} [Documented](#documented){.tada-word}
[**Accurate, detailed metadata** — typically a README — describing the code
files and their usage: environment, versions, licence, where the data are, what
runs in what order.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Annotated](#annotated){.tada-word}
[**Comments inside the code** (or code embedded in RMarkdown/Quarto alongside
descriptive text) explaining what each chunk does, why, and where its output
appears in the paper.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

## How TADA maps onto FAIR {#tada-fair}

TADA was built with the FAIR and FAIR4RS principles in mind, and each letter
maps onto one or more of them — while in two cases deliberately going further.

| FAIR principle | Definition | Covered by |
|---|---|---|
| **F**indable | Digital assets (metadata, data, code) can be easily found by both machines and humans | **Available** — provision of a unique identifier |
| **A**ccessible | Assets are retrievable via their identifier, with or without authorisation/authentication | **Available** — code is retrievable via that identifier |
| **I**nteroperable | Assets can interoperate with other assets, and are readable using standard documented formats | **Transferable** — *extended* to also mean runnable on different computers and operating systems |
| **R**eusable | Assets are described sufficiently to enable reuse and attribution, ideally via a licence | **Documented** — README plus licence |
| — | *(no direct FAIR equivalent)* | **Annotated** — internal comments, for transparency and human comprehension |

::: {.tada-note}
The **Transferable** and **Available** rows are stated in the TADA paper. The
**Documented** and **Annotated** rows are this wiki's reading: the paper defines
FAIR reusability as "sharing code in a way that clearly specifies what can be
done with it, for example, via a license and a README file", which is exactly
what Documented delivers, and it makes no FAIR claim for Annotated.
:::

Two things are worth noticing in that table.

**Transferable is broader than Interoperable.** Interoperability says anyone
can open and use your code. Transferability adds that it must also *run* on
someone else's machine and operating system — which is where hard-coded file
paths kill you.

**Annotated has no FAIR counterpart.** FAIR is largely about machines finding
and parsing assets. Annotation is about a human being able to follow what the
analysis actually did. It is the letter most specific to research code, and the
one most often skipped.

::: {.tada-note}
On "reusable": the word is used in two different senses. In the FAIR sense it
means *sharing code in a way that clearly specifies what can be done with it* —
a licence and a README. In the software-development sense it means writing
generalised, modular, tested code that runs across systems and datasets. TADA
targets the first. If you find a guideline demanding the second, check whether
it was written for software.
:::

## What TADA does not cover {#tada-scope}

The TADA paper is explicit that two things sit beyond its scope, while noting
that both support reproducible analyses:

- **Containerisation** — Docker, Singularity — which packages a complete
  software environment (programs and libraries) into an image, so that the
  environment itself is reproducible between systems. This is the standard
  answer to the "works on my computer" problem.
- **Workflow managers** — Snakemake, Nextflow — which specify the sequence of
  scripts or computational steps in a pipeline and their dependencies, so each
  step executes in a defined, reproducible order.

Neither is a requirement of TADA. Both are worth knowing about; see
[Further reading](#further-reading).

## Languages {#tada-languages}

TADA is tailored mainly to **R and Python**, because those are the open-source
languages most widely used in ecology and evolutionary biology. The basic
principles apply just as well to workflow languages (e.g. Snakemake) and
compiled languages (e.g. C++), and — as the authors note — to disciplines other
than ecology and evolutionary biology.

Where a language does not save code in a standard file type, the test to apply
is the Transferable one: **can the resulting file be opened by a plain text
editor?** SPSS syntax `.sps` files, for instance, pass that test.
